enrichment.short_title: Right-of-way Tomlin order appeal refused as futile where neighbours were not parties
key_facts: Mr and Mrs Hayes owned No.79b Melbury Gardens; access required a right of way over a driveway belonging to neighbouring No.79a (the Pedersens), originally reserved in a 1983 borough transfer but mismatched in the 1989 transfer to the Hayes.
The Hayes sued Merton rather than the Pedersens; the dispute was compromised by a Tomlin order defining an agreed route, but the Pedersens were never consulted and did not accept the route.
Rimer J construed the Tomlin order in favour of the Hayes as against the borough, while observing the ruling would have little practical value because the Pedersens were not bound.
The borough sought permission to appeal; the Court of Appeal treated the appeal as before the court, stayed enforcement of the Tomlin order, and refused permission as lacking practical utility.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Adjourned application for permission to appeal from a Chancery Division order construing a Tomlin compromise; formally granted permission, appeal heard, and order varied to stay the Tomlin order.
enrichment.outcome: Application for permission to appeal refused in substance; Tomlin order stayed; Hayes awarded costs of £2,158.50; liberty to apply.
enrichment.ratio: Where the real dispute is between neighbours over the line of a right of way and the non-neighbour parties' agreed construction cannot bind the adjoining owner, an appeal on the meaning of a Tomlin order between council and owners is of no practical value and permission should be refused; county court proceedings between the neighbours may be the appropriate forum.
legal_issues: Whether permission to appeal should be granted where the appealed construction cannot bind the adjoining landowners
Whether the Tomlin order should be stayed pending resolution between the true disputants

enrichment.short_title: Minority shareholders succeed on void patent assignment and equitable compensation against Oystertec
key_facts: Minority shareholders of Easyrad Limited brought a derivative claim challenging the 1998 assignment of the Oyster Converter patent from Easyrad to majority shareholder Paul Davidson for patent fees alone, pursuant to a 1997 Easyrad Insolvency Agreement.

Davidson floated Oystertec plc on AIM in February 2001 representing Oystertec as owner of the patent; minority investors Fraser, Barker and Davidson Tools had unsuccessfully negotiated settlement/compensation beforehand.

Pumfrey J held on summary judgment that the divestiture clause in the insolvency agreement was void as contrary to public policy and that the patent was outside the agreement in any event because it had been acquired for £50,000 not £1.
On resumed hearing, accord and satisfaction and laches defences failed; equitable compensation succeeded against Oystertec and breach of fiduciary duty succeeded against Davidson but not Binney.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Summary judgment application in derivative action proceedings permitted by Pumfrey J on 29 July 2002, with a resumed hearing on accord and satisfaction, laches/acquiescence and damages for breach of fiduciary duty.
enrichment.outcome: Claim for equitable financial compensation succeeded against Oystertec plc; claim for damages for breach of fiduciary duty succeeded at summary judgment stage against Paul Davidson but failed against Adrian Binney; permission to appeal indicated; costs and quantum to follow.
enrichment.ratio: An agreement allowing a business to be peremptorily stripped of a substantial unqualified asset on insolvency by unilateral action is void against public policy protecting creditors; where a patent assignment is ineffective, the proper remedy is equitable compensation rather than a declaration of ownership, and a controlling director who procured the assignment for personal benefit cannot show the transaction was in the company's best interests.
legal_issues: Whether the Easyrad Insolvency Agreement validly authorised divestiture of the patent on insolvency
Whether the Easyrad Assignment was void or voidable for breach of fiduciary duty
Whether minority shareholders were barred by affirmation, accord and satisfaction, or laches
Whether Oystertec and Davidson were liable in equitable compensation and/or damages

enrichment.short_title: Pilot's deceit judgment set aside where dishonesty finding was never pleaded or put to him
key_facts: DHL Air offered pilot Wells employment subject to signing a formal contract; he accepted in writing on 8 October 2001 while still employed by Virgin and began a B757 training course on 5 November without disclosing his continuing Virgin employment.
He later declined to join DHL; Virgin dismissed him after DHL contacted Virgin; DHL claimed about £13,845 for wasted training costs in contract and deceit.
The county court judge dismissed the contract claim but found deceit based on conduct at the course—a case not pleaded, not in closing submissions, and not put to Wells in cross-examination.
The Court of Appeal held Wells was prejudiced and could not uphold the crucial dishonesty finding; the respondent's notice argument on the October letter also failed.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal with permission from Reading County Court after one-day trial and written closing submissions.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; judgment entered for the defendant; costs to be assessed if not agreed.
enrichment.ratio: A finding of deceit is a grave matter requiring distinct pleading of fraud; where the judge finds dishonesty on an unpleaded basis not put to the defendant, the finding cannot stand even if much related evidence was ventilated at trial.
legal_issues: Whether the judge's finding of deceit by conduct on 5 November 2001 was procedurally valid
Whether the appellant was prejudiced by the unpleaded dishonesty finding
Whether the respondent's notice could uphold deceit based on the October acceptance letter

key_facts: The claimant appealed to the High Court against a Special Educational Needs and Disability Tribunal decision.

enrichment.outcome: Respondent ordered to pay 75% of appellant's appeal costs and costs of the costs application incurred after 16 September 2003.

enrichment.short_title: Sri Lankan claimant fails JR despite rejection of SSHD's narrow family links policy construction
key_facts: Sri Lankan claimant entered the UK clandestinely in 1998, was certified as a Dublin/third-country case returnable to Germany, and later relied on his wife and child in the UK for an Article 8 claim.

The wife had arrived separately, initially denied knowledge of the claimant, and received an initial asylum refusal in February 2001; the Secretary of State certified the November 2002 Article 8 claim as manifestly unfounded.
Kay J rejected the SSHD's novel construction that the family links policy never applied because a third-country decision had already been taken in 1998.

Nevertheless the claim failed because, even applying the 1991 policy, discretion and Article 8 proportionality would still have justified certification given the claimant's deceptive history and available reunification routes.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Application for judicial review of a section 72(2)(a) manifestly unfounded certificate in respect of an Article 8 human rights claim.
enrichment.outcome: Application for judicial review refused; usual legally aided costs assessment ordered.
enrichment.ratio: A potential third-country case may remain reviewable under the family links policy when circumstances change, but an unmeritorious immigration history and concealed family links can justify both adverse exercise of discretion under the policy and a manifestly unfounded certificate where Article 8 interference would still be proportionate.
legal_issues: Construction of the family links policy for spouses present before an initial asylum decision
Whether the Secretary of State reasonably certified the Article 8 claim as manifestly unfounded
How Adan and Aitseguer affected the claimant's earlier judicial review history

enrichment.short_title: GMC nine-month suspension upheld for inappropriate obesity drug prescribing at slimming clinic

statutes_considered.instrument: National Health Service and Health Care Professions Act 2002

key_facts: Dr Abu-Romia worked at the Image slimming clinic in Warrington and prescribed Diethylpropion to Ms A (a trading standards officer) and Ms B without adequate history-taking, non-pharmacological management, patient information, or GP notification.
Diethylpropion lacked a product licence for much of the relevant period and both patients had BMI around 27, below guideline thresholds for pharmacotherapy.

enrichment.short_title: Pharmacist's false accounting convictions upheld despite criticism of dishonesty direction
key_facts: Layean Atkinson, a Derby pharmacist, was convicted on 15 of 21 counts of false accounting relating to prescription pricing forms for nursing-home patients, fined £200 per count and ordered to pay £17,142 costs.
The prosecution case was that she knowingly submitted forms falsely claiming exemption or non-payment; her defence was carelessness under business stress after marital breakdown.

The judge directed that if she knew it was likely batch-signed forms included false declarations, that could support dishonesty; the Court of Appeal considered this direction borderline but upheld convictions viewing the summing-up as a whole.
No Ghosh direction was required; inconsistent acquittal on one count did not render other convictions unsafe.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal against conviction with leave on three grounds and renewed application on a fourth ground concerning inconsistent verdicts.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; convictions held safe; renewed application on fourth ground refused.
enrichment.ratio: For section 17(1)(a) false accounting the central issue is whether prescription forms were submitted dishonestly with a view to gain; a direction that knowing a batch likely contained false forms may support dishonesty sits near the carelessness borderline but need not render convictions unsafe when the summing-up as a whole requires knowledge of falsity, and Ghosh is unnecessary where the defence was inadvertence not honest belief.
legal_issues: Whether the judge misdirected on dishonesty by referring to likelihood in batch-signing
Whether a Ghosh direction was required
Whether acquittal on count 18 made convictions on other counts unsafe

enrichment.short_title: Chartering brokers held entitled and obliged to arbitrate commission claims under 1999 Act section 8
key_facts: Cleaves, chartering brokers, negotiated nine time charters for Nisshin each containing commission payable to Cleaves and an owners/charterers arbitration clause.
Nisshin challenged Cleaves' entitlement to commission and referred the dispute to arbitration; arbitrators held they had jurisdiction under sections 1 and 8 of the 1999 Act.
Colman J held commission clauses purporting to confer benefit on expressly identified brokers engaged section 1(1)(b), not disapplied by section 1(2), including split-commission wording.
Section 8 treated brokers as parties to the arbitration agreement for enforcement purposes by analogy with assignees taking substantive rights subject to arbitration.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Section 67 Arbitration Act 1996 application to the Commercial Court to determine whether arbitrators had jurisdiction over third-party broker commission claims.
enrichment.outcome: Application dismissed; arbitrators held to have jurisdiction; brokers entitled and obliged to arbitrate commission disputes.
enrichment.ratio: Where a charterparty commission clause purports to confer a benefit on an identified broker, section 1(1)(b) applies unless the contract clearly negates third-party enforcement; section 8 then binds the broker to the charterparty arbitration agreement when the dispute would have been arbitrable between owner and charterer, reflecting a conditional-benefit/assignment analogy rather than requiring express party intention to extend arbitration to brokers.
legal_issues: Whether Cleaves could enforce commission clauses under section 1
Whether split-commission wording conferred a separate enforceable benefit
Whether trust-of-a-promise analysis rebutted third-party enforcement after the 1999 Act
Whether section 8 subjected brokers to owners/charterers arbitration clauses

key_facts: Claimant Tariq obtained limited permission to challenge an adjudicator's purported upholding of a human rights certificate; merits grounds had already been refused permission.

enrichment.short_title: Parent may be prosecuted for pre-ESO truancy despite earlier education supervision order

statutes_considered.instrument: Criminal Justice and Court Services Act 2000

key_facts: Miss G's son failed to attend school regularly; Islington obtained an education supervision order in October 2002 after earlier warning of possible court action.
The authority later prosecuted Miss G under section 444(1A) for truancy between 29 September and 20 December 2002, relying only on the period before the ESO was made.
The appellant argued that choosing the ESO route precluded subsequent section 444 prosecution and that prosecution after the ESO was an abuse of process.
Beatson J held section 447 expressly permits prosecution as well as an ESO; reliance on pre-ESO facts was not an abuse, though post-ESO prosecution would face difficulties.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal by way of case stated from Inner London Crown Court rejecting a stay for abuse of process after magistrates' conviction under section 444(1A).
enrichment.outcome: Questions answered: (1) No—obtaining an ESO is not necessarily an abuse barring later section 444(1A) prosecution; (2) Yes—the crown court was right that there was no abuse on these facts; matter remitted to crown court.
enrichment.ratio: Section 447(1) of the Education Act 1996 contemplates prosecution instead of or as well as an education supervision order; paragraph 13 of Schedule 3 superseding the section 444 duty does not defeat an express later statutory power to prosecute for completed pre-ESO truancy, and choosing the more severe penalty route for earlier conduct is not per se an abuse of process absent manipulation or unfair representation.
legal_issues: Whether obtaining an education supervision order precludes later section 444(1A) prosecution
Interaction between Schedule 3 paragraph 13 supersession and section 447
Whether prosecution limited to pre-ESO facts amounted to abuse of process
